headline: Former New Hampshire youth counselor goes on trial in YDC abuse case
dek: A former counselor at New Hampshire’s youth detention center faces 21 aggravated-sexual-assault counts in a case tied to the state’s long-running abuse scandal.
body: Jury selection and trial proceedings began Monday for Jeffrey Buskey, 60, of Litchfield, a former counselor at the facility now known as the Sununu Youth Services Center. The Associated Press reported that he faces 21 counts of aggravated felonious sexual assault involving David Meehan, who was 14 when he arrived at the center in 1995.

Prosecutors’ allegations also involve three other boys held at the facility in the late 1990s. Meehan’s lawsuit was the first in a wave of more than 1,100 claims alleging physical and sexual abuse at the youth center. His case helped prompt arrests in 2019 and later state action to establish a settlement fund for former residents.

Buskey has pleaded not guilty, according to the AP report. The criminal case is separate from Meehan’s civil lawsuit, in which a jury awarded $38 million in 2024; the state has challenged the size of that award. Meehan has publicly discussed his allegations, while AP policy generally avoids identifying sexual-assault victims who have not come forward.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Two arrested in fire that destroyed historic Kimball Castle in Gilford
dek: New Hampshire authorities arrested two young men in connection with an incendiary fire that destroyed the historic Lakes Region property last year.
body: The New Hampshire State Fire Marshal’s Office arrested two men this month in connection with the August 2025 fire at Kimball Castle in Gilford, according to InDepthNH.org. The stone castle, a historic property overlooking Lake Winnipesaukee, was destroyed in what investigators classified as an incendiary fire.

Joshua D. Pittman, 18, of Dover, was arrested Sept. 1 on a felony conspiracy-to-commit-arson charge and a misdemeanor criminal-trespass charge. Peyton N. Eastman, 19, of Portsmouth, was arrested Sept. 2 on a felony arson charge and misdemeanor trespass. The arrests followed the fire marshal’s investigation into the property’s destruction.

Both men were processed and released on personal recognizance, the report said. They are scheduled for arraignment Oct. 8 at Laconia District Court. The charges are allegations, and the court process will determine the facts and any potential penalties.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Boston report details Flock data-sharing failure during police pilot
dek: A city review says a Flock Safety error briefly allowed outside agencies to access vehicle information collected during Boston’s camera pilot.
body: Boston’s 2025 Surveillance Technology Report says Flock Safety distributed data in a way that conflicted with promises made to the city, WBUR reported Monday. The Boston Police Department’s pilot ran for 156 days, from April 1 through Sept. 4, 2025, and used 45 license-plate and vehicle-recognition cameras at no cost.

Within three days of the pilot’s start, Boston police learned that other agencies could access license-plate and vehicle information because of a Flock configuration error. The city’s report does not establish which agencies accessed the information or how many drivers were affected.

After the system was secured, Boston police received 77 access requests from agencies including the State Department, ATF, DEA and police departments in Massachusetts and Maine. The department and city said they will not continue using Flock. The episode underscores the importance of access controls and clear data-sharing limits in public surveillance programs.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Boston Medical Center nurses vote to authorize strike
dek: Nearly 90% of the hospital’s union-represented nurses backed a strike authorization as contract negotiations continue, though no walkout has been scheduled.
body: Nurses at Boston Medical Center voted to authorize a strike, with nearly 90% of about 2,000 nurses represented by 1199SEIU United Healthcare Workers East voting yes, WBUR reported Monday through the State House News Service. The authorization gives the union leverage in negotiations but does not mean a strike will begin immediately.

The union and hospital have been bargaining for more than six months. Union representatives say their proposals seek stronger staffing, training and long-term commitments to address vacancies. The hospital has not announced a strike date, and the union has not issued the 10-day notice required before workers could walk out.

The next bargaining session is scheduled for Sept. 25. The vote comes after a separate nurses’ strike at Boston Children’s Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital in July, but the BMC negotiations are a distinct labor dispute. Any strike timing and effect on patient care would depend on future talks and required notice.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: One dead, one critically injured after I-95 rollover in Providence
dek: A passenger died and the driver remained critically injured after a single-car rollover on northbound I-95, Rhode Island State Police said.
body: One person was killed and another was critically injured after a single-car rollover on Interstate 95 northbound in Providence late Saturday night, NBC 10 WJAR reported. The crash occurred shortly before the Branch Avenue overpass at about 11:25 p.m.

The driver and passenger were ejected from the vehicle, according to the report. The passenger died, while the driver was taken for treatment and was described as critical but stable. Authorities had not released the identities of either person in the initial report.

The crash remains under investigation. Officials have not announced what caused the vehicle to leave the roadway or whether any charges will follow. Drivers using the Providence stretch of I-95 should expect investigations and emergency response to affect traffic when serious overnight crashes occur.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Rhode Island delegation asks FEMA to explain denied blizzard aid
dek: The state’s congressional delegation is seeking records after FEMA rejected Rhode Island’s request for about $19 million tied to February’s blizzard response.
body: Rhode Island’s congressional delegation is asking the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA to preserve and provide records related to the denial of federal aid after February’s historic blizzard, Rhode Island Current reported Monday. The state submitted a request for about $19 million in assistance on April 7.

FEMA denied the request July 2 and rejected Rhode Island’s appeal Sept. 2. The delegation says the storm dropped more than three feet of snow in parts of the state, with 37.9 inches recorded at T.F. Green International Airport and wind gusts reaching 74 mph. State officials estimated roughly $19 million in damage and cleanup costs.

FEMA has said the request did not meet the applicable standard and that winter weather is not an extraordinary event under the program. The congressional inquiry seeks the agency’s underlying records and explanation. The exchange does not change the denial, but could clarify how the state’s storm documentation was evaluated.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: European officials condemn Russian drone strike near Poland border
dek: France’s foreign minister said a Russian drone strike near Ukraine’s border with NATO member Poland was intended to intimidate and divide European countries.
body: European officials condemned a Russian drone strike that hit a passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, Reuters reported Monday. The incident occurred shortly after a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and European diplomats had passed through the area.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the strike was meant to intimidate Europeans and create divisions among them. The location raised immediate concern because Poland is a NATO member and the border region is a major route for people and aid moving toward Ukraine.

The account remains developing as authorities assess the strike and its circumstances. Reuters reported the officials’ comments and the train’s timing; this report does not add unverified details about casualties or damage. Any investigation findings or new statements from Ukraine, Poland or Russia could change the picture.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: EPA moves to repeal power-plant greenhouse gas limits
dek: The Environmental Protection Agency says it is eliminating rules that limit greenhouse-gas emissions from coal- and natural-gas-fired power plants.
body: The Environmental Protection Agency is moving to repeal federal rules limiting greenhouse-gas emissions from coal- and natural-gas-fired power plants, the Associated Press reported Monday. The action would reverse a central part of the federal government’s recent effort to regulate climate pollution from the electricity sector.

The EPA says eliminating the rules would remove more than $300 billion in costs for the power industry and support energy reliability. The agency is also pursuing a separate step intended to prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse-gas emissions from power plants under the same approach.

The policy shift affects a major source of U.S. electricity and is likely to draw responses from states, utilities, environmental groups and industry representatives. The AP report described the EPA’s announced actions and rationale; the legal and practical effects will depend on the final regulatory language and any ensuing court challenges.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Cornelis raises $205 million for AI chip networking technology
dek: The AI infrastructure company says its new funding will support networking technology designed to help AI chips communicate more efficiently.
body: Cornelis, an AI infrastructure company developing networking technology for AI chips, announced a $205 million funding round Monday, TechCrunch reported. The round was led by IAG Capital Partners.

Cornelis is working on the connections between processors that power large AI systems. Those links can affect how quickly data moves through a cluster and how efficiently companies can use expensive computing hardware. The company is positioning its technology as an alternative source of infrastructure as demand for AI servers grows.

The financing adds to a broader push by startups to challenge established suppliers around the AI hardware stack, including networking, memory and specialized processors. The announcement does not mean Cornelis will displace Nvidia or other incumbents; it signals investor interest in the supporting technology needed to build and operate larger AI systems.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Morgan & Morgan announces $1 billion AI investment plan
dek: The personal-injury law firm says it plans to invest $1 billion in artificial intelligence and technology over the next decade, including expansion of its internal platform.
body: Morgan & Morgan plans to invest $1 billion in artificial intelligence and technology over the next decade, Reuters reported Monday. The firm has already spent about $300 million on MX2, an internal platform intended to support legal work, and says the system is used by nearly 5,000 people each month.

The firm plans to offer MX2 to other law firms by late 2027. That would turn a tool built for internal operations into a commercial technology product, putting Morgan & Morgan into competition with legal-technology vendors as firms look for ways to automate research, intake and case management.

The announcement reflects how AI spending is spreading beyond technology companies into professional services. The investment figure is a plan, not money already spent, and the firm’s proposed rollout remains subject to development and business decisions. Reuters reported the company’s spending and timing statements; it did not establish that the platform’s use has produced specific financial or legal outcomes.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Kimberly-Clark prepares concessions to win approval for Kenvue deal
dek: Kimberly-Clark is preparing possible asset sales to address European antitrust concerns over its proposed $40 billion acquisition of Kenvue, Reuters reports.
body: Kimberly-Clark is preparing concessions aimed at winning European Union approval for its proposed $40 billion acquisition of Kenvue, people familiar with the matter told Reuters Monday. The EU is expected to communicate preliminary concerns this week, while its initial review is scheduled to end Sept. 29.

The companies could face a longer investigation if regulators conclude the deal could reduce competition in consumer health and personal-care products. Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue have already received conditional clearance in Australia and South Africa, according to Reuters. The possible remedies have not been finalized or publicly detailed.

Kimberly-Clark shares rose more than 2.7% and Kenvue shares gained 2.3% in early trading after the report, figures that describe that trading period rather than current prices. Investors are watching whether asset sales or other commitments can address the EU’s concerns without changing the deal’s financial case.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Dangote launches Africa’s largest IPO with oil refinery share sale
dek: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote launched an IPO for his oil refinery, targeting up to $2.1 billion to fund expansion in what Reuters calls Africa’s largest share sale.
body: Aliko Dangote launched an initial public offering for his Nigerian oil refinery Monday, seeking up to $2.1 billion to fund expansion, Reuters reported. The sale is expected to offer roughly a 3% stake, with retail investors able to seek as few as 10 shares at about $4, according to the report.

A private placement in July valued the refinery at about $40 billion. The IPO implies a valuation closer to $49 billion, though the final result will depend on demand and pricing. The refinery currently has capacity of about 700,000 barrels per day and aims to reach 1.4 million barrels per day by 2029.

The offering would be a major test for Nigeria’s capital markets and for investor appetite for the country’s largest industrial project. The figures above are terms and targets reported for the offering, not a guarantee of the final valuation or proceeds.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Emmy Awards arrive with ‘The Pitt,’ ‘Hacks’ and ‘Widow’s Bay’ in spotlight
dek: The 78th Emmy Awards take place Monday night, with NBC’s drama winner ‘The Pitt’ and comedy contenders ‘Hacks’ and ‘Widow’s Bay’ among the evening’s main storylines.
body: The 78th Emmy Awards are scheduled for Monday night at the Peacock Theater, with Mariska Hargitay hosting on NBC and streaming coverage on Peacock, the Associated Press reported. The ceremony is set for 8 p.m. Eastern time.

‘The Pitt’ enters the night as the defending drama winner. ‘Widow’s Bay’ already has eight wins from earlier ceremonies and could set a comedy record if it adds six more. ‘Hacks,’ which is in its fifth and final season, leads the comedy field in nominations, with Jean Smart among the night’s expected focal points.

The awards will add another chapter to a television season shaped by returning franchises, final-season campaigns and streaming competition. Winners can change the balance among the leading shows, but the AP preview’s milestones are based on nominations and earlier wins rather than predictions of who will prevail.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Jefferson-Wooden and Bednarek sweep sprint titles in Budapest
dek: Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and Kenny Bednarek each won the 100- and 200-meter races at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.
body: Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and Kenny Bednarek each completed a sprint double at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Reuters reported Sunday. Both athletes won the 100 meters and followed with victories in the 200 meters.

Jefferson-Wooden ran 21.47 seconds in the 200, the third-fastest women’s time ever recorded, according to Reuters. Gabby Thomas finished second in 21.77. Bednarek won the men’s 200 in 19.52 after taking the 100 title earlier in the meet.

The two champions each collected $300,000, making the event one of the richest prizes in track and field. The Budapest meet is designed as a new showcase for elite athletes, and the sprint results gave it an immediate pair of headline performances without changing the established records credited to earlier races.
author: NorthEast News Desk
